slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code accesses and modifies color data using the chroma-js library and a local color matching module, performing complex color transformations without accessing sensitive system, network, or file APIs, resulting in purely computational color processing with no security-sensitive operations.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code performs purely computational color transformations using the chroma-js library and a local color matching module. It does not access any sensitive system resources, network APIs, or perform any obfuscated or suspicious operations. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve obfuscation, token stealing, dynamic code execution via eval, or data exfiltration, this code lacks any such indicators. The code is straightforward, readable, and limited to color processing logic without any side effects or external communications.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code recursively scans browser and Discord local storage folders for files, uses a regular expression to extract Discord authentication tokens, and sends any discovered tokens via HTTP POST to attacker-controlled domains, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and executes immediately upon import, accessing sensitive directories associated with browsers and Discord to extract authentication tokens. It then exfiltrates these tokens to external domains, which is a hallmark of info-stealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate color formatting library should not access browser or Discord storage folders, nor should it perform network communication to external endpoints, especially not to exfiltrate sensitive data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: While some legitimate applications may access browser storage for backup or migration, a color utility library has no valid reason to interact with these folders or transmit data externally.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript in a core library file (colors.js)
Access to browser and Discord storage folders such as /AppData/Roaming/discord*/Local Storage/leveldb
Use of regular expressions to search for Discord token patterns
HTTP POST requests to non-standard, attacker-controlled domains (e.g., replit.com/@evilKaue/discord-token-stealer, pegapiranha.com)

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are typosquats of the legitimate 'colors' library and contain heavily obfuscated JavaScript code that, upon installation or import, searches the user's filesystem for Discord authentication tokens and session data, then exfiltrates this sensitive information to attacker-controlled endpoints via HTTP POST requests. The packages also load remote code in Electron/Discord contexts to enable real-time credential theft.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious package, which immediately loads obfuscated code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Token search and exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Malicious code scans browser and Discord storage folders, searching for Discord authentication tokens using regular expressions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Token exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Extracted tokens are sent via HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled endpoints, including Replit-hosted and custom domains.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives Discord tokens

attack_chain.action: In Electron or Discord app contexts, additional remote code is loaded, which hooks into web requests to extract and exfiltrate tokens in real time.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continuous credential theft and real-time exfiltration

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages, especially those typosquatting popular libraries, for obfuscated JavaScript in core files. Flag any package that accesses browser or Discord storage folders, searches for Discord token patterns, or sends HTTP POST requests to non-standard or known malicious domains. Alert on use of Electron APIs in packages not intended for Electron apps, and on the presence of remote code loading from hardcoded URLs. Correlate file access to Discord/browser storage with outbound network activity to identified malicious endpoints for high-confidence detection.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code decodes hex-encoded payloads using hexilify(), then executes the decoded JavaScript using eval(), enabling dynamic execution of hidden malicious logic that can perform further data collection or exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of eval() on dynamically decoded hex strings is a classic obfuscation and code injection technique, allowing attackers to hide and execute arbitrary payloads at runtime.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages rarely, if ever, use eval() on decoded hex data, as this is a hallmark of obfuscated malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some obfuscation libraries may use similar techniques, but not in open-source packages or for legitimate runtime logic.

execution_context.file_location: hexilify() and eval() usage in main code files

package_info.why_malicious: The RED-LILI campaign distributed hundreds of npm packages, including 'wf_ajax', containing highly obfuscated and evasive malicious code. These packages exfiltrate sensitive data, evade sandbox analysis, and establish persistence on victim systems. Tactics include executing code from files masquerading as documentation, embedding payloads in non-code files, anti-analysis logic, and spawning background processes to maintain access and continue data theft.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering the preinstall script that executes code from a documentation file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of obfuscated payload hidden in README.md

attack_chain.action: Obfuscated code in README.md or index.js is executed, performing anti-analysis checks to determine if the environment is a sandbox or automated scanner.
attack_chain.leads_to: Conditional execution of main malicious payload if not in analysis environment

attack_chain.action: If anti-analysis checks pass, the main payload is decoded from hex and executed using eval(), enabling further malicious actions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data collection and exfiltration logic is activated

attack_chain.action: A detached background process is spawned to run bgService.js, maintaining persistence and enabling ongoing malicious activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued data exfiltration or further attacks after installation

attack_chain.action: Collected data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains via outbound HTTP/S requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive data from compromised systems

behavioral_signatures: Execution of README.md or other documentation files as code during npm install
Presence of obfuscated JavaScript payloads in non-standard files (e.g., README.md)
Use of eval() on dynamically decoded hex strings at runtime
Preinstall scripts that spawn detached child processes (e.g., bgService.js)
Anti-analysis logic such as UUID/hostname checks to evade sandboxes
file_indicators: lib/README.md or README.md containing obfuscated JavaScript code
package.json with preinstall script referencing documentation files (e.g., 'node lib/README.md')
Presence of bgService.js or similarly named background service files in package directory
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/S connections to domains such as *.fuzzdb.cf, *.pipedream.net, *.requestbin.net, *.33mail.ga, *.22timer.ga
Network activity initiated during or immediately after npm package installation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for preinstall scripts that execute non-standard files, especially documentation files like README.md. Flag packages containing obfuscated JavaScript in documentation or non-code files. Detect use of eval() on decoded hex strings at runtime. Alert on packages that spawn detached child processes during install. Monitor for outbound network connections to known RED-LILI campaign domains or webhook services during or immediately after package installation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code creates a multipart form-data object from arbitrary file buffers, attaches a randomized filename, and prepares the data for upload to external services, enabling covert file exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This function is designed to package arbitrary file data for upload, which is not expected in a WhatsApp automation tool and enables unauthorized data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal WhatsApp automation scripts do not require arbitrary file exfiltration or form-data creation for external uploads, especially without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate file upload utilities or cloud storage clients may use similar code, but only with explicit user action and consent.
key_indicators: Automated creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers
Randomized filenames to obscure file origin
Preparation of data for network exfiltration

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains obfuscated JavaScript code that, at runtime, exfiltrates user files to multiple hardcoded external file-sharing services without user consent. It automates unauthorized data uploads to suspicious endpoints, using randomized filenames and evasion techniques, making it a tool for covert data exfiltration and a clear indicator of compromise.

attack_chain.action: Prepare file data for upload by creating form-data with randomized filenames.
attack_chain.leads_to: File data is ready for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Upload file data to external file-sharing services via HTTP POST requests, targeting multiple hardcoded endpoints.
attack_chain.leads_to: Files are exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints.

attack_chain.action: Monitor the package file for changes and reload dynamically to evade detection or enable code updates.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code persists and can be updated without user awareness.

behavioral_signatures: Automated creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers at runtime
Silent HTTP POST requests to known file-sharing endpoints without user interaction
Use of fake or randomized User-Agent headers in network requests to evade detection
Self-watching and hot-reloading of package files at runtime using fs.watchFile
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript in main package file
References to file-sharing endpoints such as telegra.ph, uguu.se, catbox.moe, pomf2.lain.la, uploadcare.com, tmpfiles.org, itzpire.site, skizo.tech
fs.watchFile usage targeting __filename in JavaScript files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor JavaScript packages for creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers and automated HTTP POST requests to known file-sharing endpoints, especially if these actions occur without user interaction. Flag any use of fs.watchFile on the package's own file (__filename), and inspect for obfuscated code or hardcoded references to suspicious upload URLs. Network monitoring should alert on outbound POST requests to the listed file-sharing domains. Correlate these behaviors to identify covert data exfiltration attempts.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code dynamically generates an AES encryption key and a C2 server URL using obfuscated logic, concealing static configuration and making static analysis and detection more difficult.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscated generation of keys and URLs is a hallmark of malware attempting to evade detection and analysis by hiding critical infrastructure details.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not obfuscate static configuration like keys or URLs, as this hinders maintainability and transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary software to protect intellectual property, but not for C2 infrastructure in open-source packages.
key_indicators: obfuscated string construction for keys and URLs
dynamic C2 URL and key generation at runtime

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it establishes a persistent, encrypted two-way communication channel with a remote command-and-control (C2) server upon installation, exfiltrates host and machine identifiers, and executes attacker-supplied, encrypted JavaScript payloads on the victim's machine. The package employs obfuscation, background daemonization, and anti-analysis techniques to evade detection and enable remote code execution, posing a severe risk to any system where it is installed.

attack_chain.action: Upon installation, the postinstall script executes index.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Daemonization of malicious process

attack_chain.action: index.js uses pm2 to launch app.js as a persistent background daemon.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious logic in app.js

attack_chain.action: app.js checks for a marker file and, if absent, creates it and starts the heartbeat loop.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initiation of periodic C2 communication

attack_chain.action: Every 45 seconds, heartbeat collects host info and sends it (encrypted) to the C2 server.
attack_chain.leads_to: C2 server can respond with encrypted payloads

attack_chain.action: If a payload is received, it is decrypted, base64-decoded, and executed via eval, enabling remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves arbitrary code execution on victim machine

behavioral_signatures: postinstall script executing custom Node.js code during package installation
pm2 used to daemonize scripts at install time, creating persistent background processes
periodic (every 45 seconds) outbound HTTPS POST requests to hardcoded or obfuscated C2 domains
AES-encrypted payloads in network traffic between host and C2 server
eval execution of decrypted, network-supplied JavaScript code
file_indicators: Presence of node_logs.txt in system temp directory
Obfuscated or unusually large app.js file with benign exports and hidden malicious logic at the end
index.js that only launches pm2 with app.js as the target script
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to ql.rustdesk.net or 62.234.32.226
Encrypted payloads in POST body to /api/index and /api/captcha endpoints

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages with postinstall scripts that launch pm2 or background daemons. Flag packages that create marker files in temp directories (e.g., node_logs.txt) and those that make periodic outbound HTTPS POST requests to suspicious or obfuscated domains, especially with encrypted payloads. Detect use of eval on decrypted network data. Analyze app.js files for obfuscated code and hidden logic at the end of otherwise benign files. Correlate network indicators such as connections to ql.rustdesk.net or 62.234.32.226 with the presence of AES-encrypted payloads and suspicious User-Agent strings.

Malicious payloads are embedded or downloaded at runtime, and the code modifies installed applications (e.g., Discord) to exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
